passage:
Saurabh: did you see practice today
Lakshmi: I saw you drop that one catch
Saurabh: ya. and Kunal's gang all shouted "useless!" at me
Saurabh: but when Varun from their group dropped TWO, they said "bad luck, bro, sun in your eyes"
Lakshmi: same sun for you though
Saurabh: exactly. and when Varun came late, "traffic." when I came late last week, "no discipline"
Lakshmi: that's so unfair 😠
Saurabh: I feel like whatever I do, I'm the outsider and they're the family
Lakshmi: have you told coach?
Saurabh: no. he likes them
Lakshmi: tell him anyway. or tell your dad, he'll know how to bring it up

Lakshmi: don't, bhai. your catches are better than Varun's, everyone can see that

qa.q: What did Kunal's gang shout when Saurabh dropped a catch?
qa.a: They all shouted "useless!" at him.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's wish to quit suggest he is feeling?

qa.q: What could Saurabh try instead of quitting?

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see the way Saurabh is treated?
qa.a: Lakshmi sees it clearly as unfair and angering, since the same sun and the same lateness are excused for Varun but not for Saurabh.

passage: Manoj had joined the Class 9 at the government school in Karjat in July, after his father's transfer. The boys who had been together since Class 1 sat on the last three benches and moved as one. When one of them forgot his homework, the others said, "Sir, his grandmother was ill." When Manoj forgot his, the same boys laughed. "City boy thinks he's too smart for homework." When their friend knocked over the science model, it was an accident. When Manoj's elbow brushed it, he was careless. Manoj stopped speaking in class. At lunch he ate alone near the water tank. Vasudha, who had also been new once, sat down beside him on Friday. "They did this to me in Class 6," she said. "It isn't about you." Then she walked with him to the class teacher's room to say something.

qa.q: Where did Manoj eat at lunch?
qa.a: He ate alone near the water tank.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he stopped speaking in class?
qa.a: He felt hurt and shut out, as the old group excused each other's mistakes but mocked every slip of his.

qa.q: How did Vasudha support Manoj?
qa.a: She told him it wasn't about him, sharing her own experience, and went with him to the class teacher so an adult would know.

qa.q: Why might Vasudha see the group differently from Manoj?
qa.a: Having once been the outsider herself, Vasudha sees their loyalty as a pattern of unfairness, not a sign that Manoj is bad.

grounding: Shows a new teenager outside a long-standing clique who sees its members excuse each other while judging him harshly.

passage: In Oslo, Omar's group project was due the same day as everyone else's. His was a day late because the printer broke. The popular group at the back of the class, four friends since kindergarten, handed theirs in two days late. When the teacher asked, one of them said, "We had a family thing," and the others nodded, and that was that. When Omar explained about the printer, one of the four laughed. "Sure. Printer ate your homework." Later, in the corridor, Omar heard them say he was "lazy, just like we thought." He walked home in the grey drizzle, not answering his mother's texts. Ingrid, the girl who sat next to him in maths, caught up at the bus stop. "They were two days late," she said. "I saw." Omar just shrugged. It didn't feel like enough.

qa.q: Why was Omar's project a day late?
qa.a: Because the printer broke.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling as he walked home?
qa.a: He felt hurt and discouraged, not answering texts, because the group excused their own lateness but called him lazy.

qa.q: What would you advise Omar to do next?
qa.a: Tell his mother or the teacher about the double standard, with the dates, rather than carrying it alone.

qa.q: How does Ingrid see what happened?
qa.a: Ingrid sees the unfairness clearly, noticing the group was two days late while Omar was only one.

grounding: Shows a teenager outside a clique whose members excuse their own lateness while mocking him for less.

passage: Tanvir had been in the Bengaluru hostel for two years before he noticed it. The mess committee had four paid helper posts for students. All four went to boys from the secretary's home state. The printer room key, the bike parking list, even who got the good corner rooms: it all flowed the same way. Nobody said anything unfair out loud. It just happened. One night Tanvir wrote a list on the back of a notebook: every post, every name, every state. Bhavna, from the girls' block across the road, saw it over tea. "It's the same in ours," she said. "Nobody plans it. People trust people who sound like them." At the next hostel meeting, Tanvir raised his hand, nervous. "Can we put the helper posts on the notice board, with the rules, before they're filled?" There was an awkward silence. Then the warden said, "Good idea."

qa.q: How many paid helper posts did the mess committee have?
qa.a: Four paid helper posts.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he raised his hand at the meeting?
qa.a: He felt nervous, aware that naming the pattern might upset people who never meant to be unfair.

qa.q: Which step did Tanvir take, and why is it a good first move?
qa.a: He wrote down who got each post and asked for posts and rules on the notice board, making the pattern visible and giving everyone a fair chance.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see the pattern?
qa.a: Bhavna sees it as common and unplanned, because people naturally trust those who sound like them.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that hostel jobs and help flow to people from the same region and naming the pattern as a first step to fairness.

passage:
"Pooja, have you noticed who gets the internship referrals?"
"What do you mean, Jagdish?"
"Every alumni referral this year went to students from the same two colleges the seniors came from."
"Maybe they're just better?"
"Maybe. But the girl from our college with the best project didn't even get a call."
"Hmm. My cousin says it's like that everywhere. People help people from their own place."
"I don't think anyone's doing it on purpose."
"No. They just trust their own."
"So what do we do? Complain?"
"First, just say it out loud. At the placement meeting. 'Are referrals open to everyone? Is there a list of criteria?'"
"They might get annoyed."
"Maybe. But if nobody names it, it'll keep happening, and nobody will even see it."

qa.q: Where did every alumni referral go this year?
qa.a: To students from the same two colleges the seniors came from.

qa.q: What seems to bother Jagdish about the referrals?
qa.a: Jagdish feels uneasy and a bit frustrated that the best project got no call, while believing nobody is doing it on purpose.

qa.q: What does Jagdish plan to do first, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Ask at the placement meeting whether referrals are open to all and what the criteria are, which names the pattern without accusing anyone.

qa.q: How might the student with the best project see the referrals?
qa.a: She may feel overlooked and confused, since her strong work didn't even earn a call.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that internship help flows to people from the same colleges and planning to name the pattern.

passage: In my first year at the Pune hostel, I did something I only noticed later. I'm Jahnavi, from Nagpur, and I found the other Marathi-speaking girls on day one. We shared pickles, notes, and scooter rides. When one of us needed a lab partner, we asked each other. When Darshan, a boy from Assam, asked in the corridor if anyone had last year's physics notes, I said, "Sorry, don't know." I did have them. I just didn't know him. It took me a year to see the pattern. The help in our hostel flowed along languages, like water finding old channels. Nobody meant harm. But Darshan spent that term alone in the library. In second year, I put my notes on the common drive for everyone, and I told my friends why. Naming it felt awkward. Not naming it had been worse.

qa.q: What did Darshan ask for in the corridor?
qa.a: He asked if anyone had last year's physics notes.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on seeing the pattern a year later?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt uncomfortable and a little guilty, realising the help had flowed only to people who spoke the same language.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do in second year, and why was it fair?
qa.a: Jahnavi put the notes on the common drive for everyone and explained why to friends, opening help beyond one group.

qa.q: What was that first term like for Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan spent that term alone in the library, left out of the help that flowed between language groups.

grounding: A student looks back on noticing that help in Jahnavi's hostel flowed along language lines, including Jahnavi's own, and naming the pattern.

passage: Thanks for having me, Ira. So, I'm Gurleen, and last year I hired for my team for the first time. And the first thing I noticed? I liked every candidate from my own college. Same jokes, same professors, I felt at home in five minutes. That scared me a little. So I made three rules for myself. One: write down the criteria before reading any CV. Two: make sure the shortlist had people who didn't look or sound like me. I asked a colleague from a different city to find two extra candidates. Three: before every decision, I asked myself, "Would I say the same if this person was from my college?" One candidate from a small-town college, very quiet, scored highest on the actual tasks. My gut wanted the other one. I hired the quiet one. She's our best analyst now.

qa.q: How many rules did Gurleen make for hiring?
qa.a: Three rules.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling on liking every candidate from the same college?
qa.a: Gurleen felt a little scared, worried that comfort with familiar people was steering her choices.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen's rules seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Asking "Would I say the same if this person was from my college?" before each decision, because it tests the call directly for in-group bias.

qa.q: How might the quiet candidate from the small-town college have been affected without these rules?
qa.a: She might have lost the job to a more familiar candidate, despite scoring highest on the actual tasks.

grounding: Shows a young professional using clear criteria, seeking candidates unlike Gurleen, and checking each call against own-group bias.

passage: I was taking notes at the planning meeting when Chetan read out his list of speakers for the conference. Six names. I knew at least four; they were his batchmates. Bhavna listened, nodded, and then did something I'd never seen a chair do. She asked everyone to write the selection criteria on the whiteboard first: expertise, fresh ideas, a mix of regions, a new voice. Then she put Chetan's six beside the criteria. Two fitted well. Four were friends of friends. She didn't say that. She just asked, "Who's missing?" Someone mentioned a researcher from Guwahati. Someone else, a woman who ran a rural lab. Bhavna added them. Then she said, "Let's check: would we pick these same people if none of us knew them?" Chetan went red, but he nodded. The final list kept two of his names.

qa.q: How many speakers were on Chetan's list?
qa.a: Six names.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt when he went red?
qa.a: Chetan probably felt embarrassed, seeing that most of his picks were friends rather than the best fits for the criteria.

qa.q: What made Bhavna's approach fair?
qa.a: She set clear criteria first, asked who was missing, and checked whether they'd choose the same people as strangers.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna ask "Who's missing?" instead of criticising Chetan's list?
qa.a: She seemed calm and fair-minded, wanting to widen the list without shaming Chetan in front of everyone.

grounding: An observer describes a chair using clear criteria, seeking people outside the group, and checking picks for in-group favouritism.

passage:
Monday. Hansa had to choose one person from her team to lead the new client project. Her first thought was Kiran, who had studied at her college and laughed at her jokes. She wrote the name down, then stopped.
Wednesday. She listed what the project needed: client handling, budgeting, patience with delays. She scored each of her five team members against it, using examples from the last year. Rafiq, who had come from a smaller firm and rarely spoke in meetings, scored highest. Kiran came third.
Friday. Before announcing, Hansa asked herself one more question: if Rafiq had been from her college and Kiran hadn't, would she hesitate? She wouldn't. She called Rafiq in. He looked surprised. "Why me?" She showed him the list. "Because of this," she said. Later she told Kiran the same, with the same list.

qa.q: How many team members did Hansa score against the list?
qa.a: Her five team members.

qa.q: What might Hansa have felt when she stopped after writing Kiran's name?
qa.a: She seemed uneasy, suspecting that liking Kiran and sharing a college was guiding her more than the project's needs.

qa.q: Why was showing the list to both Rafiq and Kiran a good step?
qa.a: It made the decision transparent and based on clear criteria, so neither could see it as favouritism.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel being chosen?
qa.a: Rafiq seemed surprised at first, likely also pleased and respected, since he rarely spoke up and wasn't in the familiar group.

grounding: Shows a team lead using clear criteria and checking whether she'd make the same call if the person belonged to her own group.

passage: In Class 3, Miss made Usha stand outside the classroom for the whole maths period. I'm Chandrika, and I remember thinking, Usha must be very bad. Only bad children stand outside. I didn't sit with her at lunch. I told my mother that Usha was naughty. The next day, Miss said sorry to Usha in front of everyone. It was another girl who had torn the chart paper. Usha hadn't done anything. I felt strange in my stomach. I had been so sure. My mother said, "Sometimes things happen to people who didn't do anything wrong." I didn't like that. It felt scary. If Usha could be punished for nothing, so could I. But I sat with Usha at lunch after that, and I gave her half my paratha.

qa.q: What did Miss say to Usha the next day?
qa.a: Miss said sorry to Usha in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika feel strange in her stomach?
qa.a: Chandrika felt uneasy and a little ashamed, having been so sure Usha was bad just because she was punished.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do after learning the truth, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Chandrika sat with Usha at lunch and shared a paratha, treating her kindly instead of as someone who deserved punishment.

qa.q: What was the maths period like for Usha?
qa.a: Usha had to stand outside for the whole period for something she hadn't done, and then lost friends at lunch too.

grounding: A child looks back on believing a punished classmate must have been bad, because fairness felt like the rule of the world.

passage:
Class 5, Monday. Teacher's note.
Vandana's new bicycle was stolen from the school stand on Friday. This morning Pranav told his group, "It happened because she's always talking in class. God punished her." Vandana heard it and went very quiet.
I asked Pranav to stay back. "Do you think only naughty people lose things?" He said yes, because that is fair. I asked if he remembered when his own tiffin was stolen last year. He did. "Were you naughty?" He shook his head, looking unsure.
We talked about how bad things can happen to good people, and that thinking otherwise can hurt them twice. I've also informed the principal about the theft and asked for a lock at the stand. Tomorrow, circle time on this.

qa.q: What happened to Vandana's new bicycle?
qa.a: It was stolen from the school stand on Friday.

qa.q: Why does Pranav believe Vandana deserved the theft?
qa.a: He feels that the world should be fair, so it seems to him that only naughty people lose things, which feels safer to believe.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: The teacher reminded Pranav of his own stolen tiffin, talked about bad things happening to good people, and asked for a lock, protecting Vandana and teaching fairness.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel hearing Pranav's comment?
qa.a: Vandana probably feels hurt and ashamed, blamed on top of losing her new bicycle.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child believing a classmate's stolen bicycle was a punishment for being naughty, because fairness feels like the rule of the world.

passage:
Dear diary,
The big rain came on Tuesday and flooded Indu aunty's house at the end of our lane. Her sofas and books got wet. Today I told Nani that Indu aunty must be a bad person, because God only sends floods to bad people. I'm Chaitanya, and I was sure of it.
Nani stopped peeling peas. She said Indu aunty is the kindest person in our lane, and her house is just the lowest one. The water goes there first. "Rain doesn't check who is good," Nani said.
Then I felt bad.
In the evening Nani and I took her a flask of tea and helped carry her books to the roof to dry. She hugged me. She did not look like a bad person at all.

qa.q: Why did the water go to Indu aunty's house first, according to Nani?
qa.a: Her house is just the lowest one.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling after Nani's answer?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt bad and a little ashamed, remembering how kind Indu aunty had always been.

qa.q: What did Nani and Chaitanya do, and why was it the right response?
qa.a: They took Indu aunty tea and helped dry her books, supporting her instead of blaming her for bad luck.

qa.q: How might Indu aunty feel when Chaitanya and Nani came to help?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and grateful, hugging Chaitanya after a hard, sad day.

grounding: A child's diary shows the belief that a flood must have punished a bad person, until the grandmother explains that rain doesn't choose.

passage: In Sangli, Himani's phone was snatched at the bus stand on Saturday evening. A boy on a motorbike grabbed it from her hand and was gone. By Monday, the story had gone round Class 11. Deepak, leaning on the classroom door, said loudly, "Well, she was showing it off. What did she expect?" A few boys laughed. Himani was at her desk. She put her head down. Deepak felt a flash of something uncomfortable, then pushed it away. It was her fault, he told himself. If she'd been careful, it wouldn't have happened. And he was careful, so it wouldn't happen to him. At break, the class teacher, who had heard, called Deepak aside. "Himani was holding her phone at a bus stand, like everyone does. Would it be your fault if it were you?" Deepak had no answer.

qa.q: What did Deepak say about Himani's phone?
qa.a: "Well, she was showing it off. What did she expect?"

qa.q: Why did Deepak push away the uncomfortable feeling?
qa.a: Believing Himani caused it let him feel safe, since he was careful and so, he told himself, it couldn't happen to him.

qa.q: How did the class teacher respond, and why was it useful?
qa.a: The teacher called Deepak aside the same day and asked whether it would be his fault if it happened to him, challenging the blame.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Himani?
qa.a: Himani, already shaken by the theft, had to hear classmates laugh at her, so she put her head down in shame.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming a classmate for being robbed, which lets him believe he is safe, until a teacher questions it.

passage: After school in Leeds, Jamal and his friends were talking about Dalia, who had been getting nasty comments online all week. "She posts too much," Jamal said, kicking a stone. "If you put yourself out there, that's what you get." His friends shrugged. Jamal liked that idea. He didn't post much. So it wouldn't happen to him. That evening his older sister showed him something on her phone. Dalia had told her form tutor that morning, and the school had already contacted the parents of the students who'd written the comments. "It's the people writing them who did it, not her," his sister said. "Would you say the same if someone went after you?" Jamal felt his face heat up. He thought about what he'd said at the bus stop, and who had heard.

qa.q: Who had Dalia told about the comments?
qa.a: Dalia had told her form tutor that morning.

qa.q: Why did Jamal like the idea that Dalia caused the comments?
qa.a: It made him feel safe and in control, since he didn't post much, so it seemed it couldn't happen to him.

qa.q: What went wrong in Jamal's thinking, and what could fix it?
qa.a: He blamed the victim to feel safe; he could put the blame on the people writing the comments and support Dalia instead.

qa.q: How did the school respond after Dalia spoke to her tutor?
qa.a: The school had already contacted the parents of the students who wrote the comments that same day.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming a classmate for online bullying to feel safe himself, while the school acts on her report.

passage: On Thursday night, Jomon's wallet disappeared from his room in the boys' hostel of the Kottayam school. His door had been open while he showered. At breakfast Harish said, loud enough for everyone, "Leave your door open and cry when things vanish. Your fault, man." Jomon stared at his idli. Harish felt good saying it. If it was Jomon's carelessness, then Harish, who always locked up, was safe. That afternoon the warden called a meeting. Two other rooms had been robbed the same night, and one of them had been locked. "Whoever did this is responsible," the warden said. "Not the boys who lost things." Harish shifted on the bench. His own room was one of the two others. He had been robbed too, and he hadn't even noticed yet.

qa.q: How many other rooms had been robbed the same night?
qa.a: Two other rooms.

qa.q: Why did Harish feel good blaming Jomon at breakfast?
qa.a: It made him feel safe and superior, believing that a careful boy who locked up could not be robbed.

qa.q: How did the warden respond, and why was it important?
qa.a: The warden called a meeting that afternoon and said the thief was responsible, not the boys who lost things, which put the blame where it belonged.

qa.q: What was breakfast like for Jomon?
qa.a: Jomon, already upset about his wallet, was shamed in front of everyone and just stared at his idli.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming a robbed hostel-mate to feel safe himself, until he learns his own locked room was robbed too.

passage: When Hemant came back to Satara after three weeks in hospital with typhoid, he expected sympathy. At the tea stall, an uncle said, "Must be all that outside food you students eat." At home, an aunt said, "God is teaching you to pray more." His exam results had suffered too, and a neighbour said, "Maybe you weren't serious." Each comment stung more than the fever had. He stopped going out. He told his friends he was busy. When his friend Pankaj came by, Hemant said little. Pankaj sat on the step anyway. "Illness isn't a report card, Hemant. My father got typhoid from the village well, and he's the most careful man I know." Hemant looked up. "Everyone says it's my fault." "Everyone's wrong," Pankaj said. "And your doctor said so too, didn't he?" Hemant nodded slowly.

qa.q: How long was Hemant in hospital?
qa.a: Three weeks, with typhoid.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as the comments piled up?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and hurt, as if the illness were his fault, so he withdrew and stopped going out.

qa.q: How did Pankaj support Hemant?
qa.a: Pankaj sat with him, told him illness isn't a report card, shared his father's story, and reminded him the doctor also said it wasn't his fault.

qa.q: How might the uncle and aunt see their comments?
qa.a: They may think they are just explaining or advising, not seeing that blaming him adds shame to his pain.

grounding: Shows a young adult who fell ill hearing people say he caused it, which adds shame and pushes him into silence.

passage: Wei was on the late train home from the university in Manchester when two men started shouting at him about his face and where he came from. Nobody in the carriage said anything. He got off two stops early and walked the rest in the rain, shaking. At the flat, one flatmate listened and said, "Did you say something to them first? People don't usually just do that." Wei went to his room and closed the door. He didn't mention it again for a week. It was Lucia, from his seminar group, who noticed he'd stopped taking the late train. When he finally told her, she didn't ask what he'd done. "That's on them, not you," she said. That afternoon she walked with him to the student welfare office, and they helped him report it and arranged someone to talk to.

qa.q: Where did Wei get off the train?
qa.a: He got off two stops early and walked the rest in the rain.

qa.q: What was Wei feeling after his flatmate's question?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and hurt, as if he were being blamed, so he shut himself away and stayed silent for a week.

qa.q: What did Lucia do that helped?
qa.a: She placed the blame on the attackers, not Wei, and went with him that afternoon to the welfare office to report it and get support.

qa.q: How might the flatmate's question have seemed to the flatmate?
qa.a: The flatmate may have thought it a reasonable question, not realising it suggested Wei deserved the abuse.

grounding: Shows a young adult harassed on a train meeting a flatmate who hints he provoked it, adding shame, until a friend and the welfare office support him.

passage: The results board outside the engineering hostel office showed Chaitanya had failed two subjects. By evening, the story in the corridor was already fixed. "He must have been partying," said Jeevan, a senior. "People who fail usually deserve it." Nobody knew Chaitanya's father had been in and out of hospital all semester, and that he had spent most weekends on the night bus home. He didn't tell them. He lay in bed and let them think it. For a week he skipped the mess and ate biscuits in his room. Then the hostel warden, who had heard the corridor talk, knocked on his door. "Chaitanya, the college counsellor has time today. I'll walk you there." At the counsellor's office he finally said it all. The counsellor listened, then helped him apply for a supplementary exam with a medical note from his father's doctor.

qa.q: How many subjects had Chaitanya failed?
qa.a: He had failed two subjects.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya stay silent and skip the mess?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and alone, hearing people say he deserved to fail, so he hid rather than explain his father's illness.

qa.q: How did the warden and counsellor help Chaitanya?
qa.a: The warden walked him to the counsellor the same day, and the counsellor listened and helped him apply for a supplementary exam.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel if he learned about Chaitanya's father?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel embarrassed and sorry, realising his quick judgement had added to Chaitanya's pain.

grounding: Shows a student who failed after a hard semester hearing others say he deserved it, which pushes him into silence until adults step in.

passage: I worked two desks from Minakshi when the layoffs came. Darshan, from our team, was one of the twelve let go. By lunch, people were whispering: "He must have been underperforming." "They don't cut good people." I'd half thought the same, I'm ashamed to say. It made the whole thing feel less random, and less scary for the rest of us. Minakshi didn't join in. She walked straight over to Darshan's desk and helped him pack his plant and photo frame into a box. She said, loudly enough, "You were cut because the whole project was cut. Your work was good." That evening she sent him three job leads. The next week, at the team meeting, she asked the manager to explain the criteria for the cuts in writing, so nobody would be left guessing or blaming.

qa.q: How many people were let go in the layoffs?
qa.a: Twelve were let go.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi walk straight over to Darshan's desk?
qa.a: She seemed caring and firm, wanting to support him and stop the idea that he had deserved to lose his job.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do to support Darshan and push for fairness?
qa.a: She helped him pack, said his work was good, sent job leads, and asked the manager to explain the layoff criteria in writing.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when Minakshi spoke up for him?
qa.a: Darshan probably felt less ashamed and more supported, hearing publicly that he was cut because the project was cut.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague who accepts that bad things happen to good workers, supports the one laid off, and pushes for fair criteria.

passage:
Sunday. Arohi's flat was burgled while she was at her sister's wedding. Laptop, jewellery, her grandmother's watch. A neighbour said, "Should've got a better lock." Sarika, her friend from work, arrived with dinner and sat on the floor among the mess with her. "You didn't do this. Someone else did."
Wednesday. Arohi kept blaming herself. Sarika didn't argue; she just listened, and helped her file the police report and call her insurance company. She also noticed the lane had no working street light, and the building gate never closed.
The next Saturday. Sarika had collected twenty signatures from the building and taken them to the ward office, asking for the street light to be fixed and the gate repaired. Arohi walked beside her, holding the file. "For whoever lives here next," Sarika said.

qa.q: What was stolen from Arohi's flat?
qa.a: Laptop, jewellery, her grandmother's watch.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was still blaming herself and felt guilty, as if the burglary were somehow her fault.

qa.q: What did Sarika do, and why was it a mature response?
qa.a: She supported Arohi without blame, helped with the police report and insurance, then collected signatures for a street light and gate repair to make things fairer for everyone.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's comment about the lock have affected Arohi?
qa.a: It likely added to Arohi's guilt, suggesting the burglary was her own fault.

grounding: Shows a mature friend accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting the victim of a burglary, and working to make the lane safer.

passage: Abhinav, you asked why I get angry when people say someone "deserved" their bad luck. Let your Damini Maasi tell you. When I was twenty-five, in Jabalpur, my neighbour Kusum's husband was hit by a truck on the highway. A good man, honest, kind to every child in the lane. At the funeral, I heard an old woman whisper, "Must be the sins of a past life." Kusum heard it too. Her face changed. Something in me said, no. I sat with Kusum every evening for a month. I didn't give her reasons. I just held her hand. And then I did one more thing. That turning had killed three people in two years. I went with the other women to the collector's office, again and again, until they put in a speed breaker and a light. Nobody deserved that road.

qa.a: Sitting with Kusum every evening without giving reasons, and going to the collector's office until a speed breaker and a light were put in.

qa.q: How might Kusum have felt when she heard the whisper?
qa.a: Kusum's face changed, suggesting she felt wounded and ashamed on top of her grief.

grounding: An elder recalls supporting a grieving neighbour without blame, accepting that bad things happen to good people, and working to fix a dangerous road.

passage: At the Monday assembly in the Indore school, Jagdish had to walk up the stage steps to receive the drawing prize. On the second step his foot slipped and he stumbled, catching himself on the railing. He got the certificate, walked back to his line and stared at his shoes, face burning. The whole school had seen. Four hundred children. They would laugh about it for the rest of the year. He didn't go to the canteen at break. At lunch, Noor sat down beside him. "Congratulations on the prize! Your drawing was the one with the elephant, na?" Jagdish mumbled, "Did you see me fall?" Noor looked blank. "You fell? When?" grounding: Shows a child sure the whole school saw his stumble and will remember it, while a classmate never even noticed.

passage: Manoj, you're hiding because you said the wrong answer in class? Come here, sit with your Indu Nani. When I was nine, in Mysore, I was in the Dasara dance programme at school.
